Subject: Transit conduit strategy: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Hi Tom —

Thanks again for the call yesterday. As discussed, I wanted to lay out the three ingress/egress options we typically see for Redwood Private deployments and capture what matters for NetLinx: latency, throughput, security posture (zero-trust / egress filters), and operational cost.

Attached: redwood-topology-diff.pdf (visual comparison) and a rough cost sketch (netlinx-cost-estimate.xlsx).

Quick summary:
- VPC Peering: low-latency, simple routing, but limits cross-account control (no AWS PrivateLink-style endpoint isolation). Works well for single-account setups or when both sides can accept route table changes.
- AWS/Cloud PrivateLink (endpoint services): strong isolation, per-service ACLs, good for multi-tenant or tightly restricted egress policies; slightly higher egress cost and extra NAT/ENI management.
- Site-to-Site VPN (S2S): easiest to onboard from customer's network, but has variable latency and additional management for tunnels (BGP, HA tunnels). Good for proof-of-concept and constrained environments.

Open questions for us to resolve:
1) Do you need mutual TLS + mTLS client certs for every connection, or will IP allowlisting + PrivateLink be sufficient?
2) Expected request volume and percent low-latency (<50ms) traffic.
3) Any procurement or network change constraints on your side (e.g., no cross-account peering allowed)?

Proposed next step: 30-min architecture review this week where Karthik walks through the topology and we map NetLinx traffic patterns to the right pattern. Are you available Thu 20th 10:00–10:30 PT?

Tom — quick technical take ahead of Thu's call.

(1) If NetLinx can accept cross-account peering and route changes, VPC Peering gives the simplest topology and the best latency profile — it’s pure L3 routing with no extra proxy hops. For your 60% latency-sensitive traffic I expect Peering will reduce P99 tail by ~12–18ms vs an S2S gateway in many of our benchmarks. Downside: peering doesn't give per-service ACLs and requires shared routing ownership.

(2) PrivateLink (we call it endpoint-service on our side) is the best fit if you need strict tenancy/security controls. You get per-endpoint ENIs in your VPC, and we can restrict access to specific services (embedding API vs generation API). Cost: ENI and data processing fees; also slightly higher egress-cost compared to peering due to managed endpoint pricing. For 1.2k RPS, our rough estimate (see Sean's attachment) shows a ~15–25% delta vs peering on per-token egress costs, depending on region. Operationally this removes the need to touch route tables but requires managing endpoint security groups and potentially a NAT for outbound calls.

(3) S2S VPN is pragmatic for early POCs or customers with strict on-prem constraints. It's the slowest and most operationally heavy (BGP flaps, MTU issues) and should be treated as a transitional solution unless you need it long-term.

Recommendation: For NetLinx I suggest a hybrid approach: start with PrivateLink for production traffic carrying PII (mTLS + endpoint SGs) and keep a peered VPC for high-throughput, low-latency bulk traffic (analytics) to optimize cost. Use S2S only for legacy on-prem integrations that cannot change.

I'll include a 5-slide latency & cost delta in Thu's deck.
